Massive New Moon Crater Discovered by NASA: Inside the 'Once-in-a-Century' Asteroid Impact

In a planetary science breakthrough that rewrites our understanding of the lunar surface, NASA scientists have confirmed the discovery of the largest newly formed impact crater ever recorded across the modern solar system. Dubbed the McGetchin crater, the colossal chasm measures roughly 728 feet (222 meters) wide and up to 141 feet (43 meters) deep—the result of a rare once-in-a-century asteroid collision.

✍️ By: NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter & Planetary Defense Team 📅 Published: September 17, 2026 ⏱️ Read Time: 8 min read

1.1. Quick Facts: The McGetchin Crater Discovery

In a planetary science breakthrough that rewrites our understanding of the lunar surface, NASA scientists have confirmed the discovery of the largest newly formed impact crater ever recorded across the modern solar system.

Dubbed the McGetchin crater, the colossal chasm measures roughly 728 feet (222 meters) wide and up to 141 feet (43 meters) deep—spanning the equivalent of two full football fields and plunging deep enough to vertically stack three yellow school buses.

Published in a pair of research papers in the journal Science Advances, the discovery was made by image-processing specialist Robert Wagner while conducting routine data-quality checks on high-resolution maps gathered by NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO).

The planetary strike, which occurred between April 11 and May 22, 2024, was caused by a comet or asteroid fragment the size of a three- to six-story building smashing into the Moon's eastern limb. According to NASA impact probability models, a collision of this magnitude is a statistically rare, "once-in-a-lifetime" phenomenon that occurs only once every 132 years.

Key facts at a glance: • Crater Name: McGetchin Crater (named in honor of pioneering lunar volcanologist Dr. Thomas R. McGetchin). • Dimensions: 728 feet (222 meters) in diameter, 141 feet (43 meters) deep. • Impact Window: Occurred between April 11 and May 22, 2024. • Impactor Size: Estimated comet or asteroid rocky projectile measuring between 30 and 60 feet across (comparable to a three- to six-story building). • Primary Discovery Facility: NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), utilizing both the Wide-Angle Camera (WAC) and Narrow-Angle Camera (NAC). • Thermal Signature: Uncovered a massive 4-mile-wide (6.5 km) "cold spot" where disturbed regolith loses heat rapidly at night. • Frequency of Occurrence: Estimated to occur only once every 100 to 132 years. • Core Scientific Publications: Two peer-reviewed research papers published in Science Advances on September 16, 2026.

2.2. The Accidental Discovery: How Robert Wagner Spotted the Anomaly

The historic discovery began not during an active planetary defense watch, but during a routine photographic data-quality sweep.

Robert Wagner, an image-processing specialist from Intuitive Machines working with the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) team, was analyzing automated lunar change-detection maps. Since its orbital insertion in 2009, the LRO has continuously looped from pole to pole roughly 60 miles above the lunar surface. To detect surface evolution, automated algorithms stack hundreds of multi-year "before" and "after" frames: regions that remain static render as neutral grey, while active topographic shifts appear as bright or dark pixels.

Because orbital change-detection algorithms frequently trigger hundreds of false alarms caused by minor shifts in solar illumination angles and shadow lengths, Wagner manually inspects suspect coordinates.

On October 24, 2025, while scanning a global mosaic, an enormous bright spot encircled by a distinct, dark halo on the Moon's eastern edge caught his attention:

"I just stopped, dropped everything, and started looking into what that spot was," Wagner recalled. "It was by far the most obvious impact debris pattern I've ever seen in one of these images."

Upon switching from the low-resolution Wide-Angle Camera to the high-resolution Narrow-Angle Camera—capable of resolving surface details down to 3 feet (1 meter) per pixel—the true scale of the impact became apparent. Wagner had located a fresh, steep-sided crater three times larger than the previous record-holding impact spotted by LRO a decade prior.

3.3. High-Velocity Ballistics: 100 Kilometers of Churned Surface

The cosmic projectile struck the lunar surface with intense kinetic energy, vaporizing on impact and sending shockwaves rippling through the brittle lunar crust.

Unlike Earth, where a dense atmosphere incinerates space rocks smaller than a football field, the airless vacuum of the Moon leaves its surface defenseless against incoming debris.

Data analyzed by Mark Robinson, chief scientist for the LROC system and lead author of the primary Science Advances study, revealed surprising ejecta dynamics:

• Asymmetric Blast Zone: Impact debris and excavated pulverized rock, known as ejecta, churned and scarred the lunar surface across a radius exceeding 66 miles (100 kilometers). • Steep Ejection Angles: Soil and pulverized basaltic rock fragments were hurled outward at significantly steeper vertical trajectories than standard impact cratering models predicted, indicating unique subsurface density resistance or atypical projectile impact angles. • The Bright Ray System: The brilliant white splash surrounding the crater represents freshly excavated, unweathered subsurface regolith, which has not yet been darkened by millions of years of exposure to the harsh solar wind and cosmic radiation.

4.4. The 4-Mile 'Cold Spot': Thermal Changes in the Lunar Regolith

The physical crater rim tells only half of the scientific story. In a companion study published simultaneously in Science Advances, scientists working with LRO's thermal radiometer instrument, Diviner, revealed that the impact altered the thermal conductivity of the surrounding Moon across miles.

Between November 2025 and February 2026, Diviner scanned the impact zone during the freezing two-week lunar night. The data revealed a sprawling, 4-mile-wide (6.5 km) "cold spot" surrounding the crater where nighttime temperatures dropped approximately 16 degrees Fahrenheit (roughly 9 degrees Celsius) colder than adjacent unaffected terrain.

Why Did the Ground Become Colder? The localized drop in temperature occurs due to mechanical displacement of the lunar soil:

• Regolith Compaction vs. Porosity: Over billions of years, micrometeoroid bombardment compresses ancient lunar regolith into a moderately dense, semi-cohesive matrix capable of storing solar heat during the daytime and slowly radiating it outward at night. • The "Fluffing" Effect: The violent shockwave and falling ejecta rain from the McGetchin strike decompressed and "fluffed up" the top layers of soil, increasing porosity and drastically reducing its bulk density. • Loss of Thermal Inertia: Because fluffy, aerated regolith acts like loose, powdery snow, it exhibits low thermal inertia—losing absorbed daytime heat almost immediately after sunset.

This finding carries vital engineering implications for upcoming robotic and crewed missions: loose, low-density regolith directly alters how rover mobility systems grip the soil, increasing the risk of mechanical slip or wheel entrapment.

5.5. Overturning Apollo Assumptions: How Dynamic Is the Moon?

For decades, the cultural perception of the Moon has been one of timeless, static desolation—a frozen museum where human footprints left by Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin would remain pristine for billions of years.

The catalog of fresh craters amassed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter over the past 17 years has fundamentally dismantled that myth.

According to Mark Robinson, LRO observations indicate that the uppermost inch (2.5 centimeters) of lunar soil is continuously overturned, churned, and buried by ballistic ejecta roughly every 80,000 years—a geological process operating much faster than pre-mission planetary models estimated. Consequently, the Apollo landing sites and footprints will be entirely erased on cosmic timescales.

6.6. Protecting NASA's Artemis Moon Base

The confirmation of the McGetchin crater arrives at a pivotal juncture as NASA, international space agencies, and commercial aerospace contractors prepare to deploy permanent infrastructure on the Moon under the Artemis program.

With NASA aiming to establish an enduring lunar habitat at the lunar South Pole, the data provided by McGetchin offers critical empirical metrics for planetary defense and structural habitat shielding:

• Secondary Crater Hazards: When a large asteroid strikes the Moon, secondary impacts caused by hurled rock fragments can pepper surrounding terrain for dozens of miles, threatening solar arrays, pressurized crew modules, and propellant storage depots. • Risk Probability Calculations: Understanding that 200-meter craters occur once per century allows mission planners to calculate statistical structural damage probabilities for 30-year lunar surface bases. • Subsurface Foundation Design: The discovery of expansive "cold spots" demonstrates that habitats cannot simply be anchored into the topsoil; foundation pilings must penetrate deep into undisturbed bedrock to ensure mechanical stability.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

Q1: What is the McGetchin crater?

The McGetchin crater is a newly formed, 728-foot-wide (222-meter) and 141-foot-deep (43-meter) impact crater discovered on the Moon by NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO). It is the largest fresh impact crater ever observed in the modern solar system.

Q2: When did the asteroid hit the Moon?

Planetary scientists determined that the comet or asteroid struck the eastern limb of the Moon between April 11 and May 22, 2024, as verified through temporal constraints from LRO orbital passes.

Q3: How often do large asteroids hit the Moon?

While roughly 140 small impact craters (around 30 feet wide) form on the Moon annually, large impacts capable of carving 200-meter-wide craters like McGetchin occur only once every 100 to 132 years.

Q4: Will astronaut footprints last forever on the Moon?

No. Because impact ejecta churns and overturns the top inch (2.5 centimeters) of lunar regolith roughly every 80,000 years, all human footprints and hardware left behind by Apollo astronauts will eventually be buried and eroded away on cosmic timescales.
